strengths: Addresses an underexplored niche—combining learned optimization with second-order (SR1) quasi-Newton structure—rather than the more commonly studied first-order learned optimizers.

The limited-memory, buffer-based rank-one construction (Eq. 7) is a sensible way to keep the learned preconditioner PSD by construction while retaining scalability across problem dimensions, and the element-wise MLP design gives dimension invariance, which is empirically tested by training on small N and testing on larger N.

Reasonably broad experimental suite: controlled quadratic ablations isolating the effect of the projection term, performance-profile comparisons against LBFGS/Adam/AdaHessian on a battery of benchmark functions, and a real downstream application (HMR on 3DPW).

Good engineering transparency: detailed appendices with architecture tables, hyperparameters, ablations on encoder inputs/hidden size, and runtime/memory profiling, which aids reproducibility even though code is not yet released.

The HMR results show a smaller model (10.4M vs 17.4M parameters) reaching lower PA-MPJPE than the LGD baseline without task-specific fine-tuning, which is a meaningful practical selling point if the efficiency claims hold up.
weaknesses: The central 'learned projection' is somewhat misleadingly named: Eq. (8) is not an operator applied at inference to project a candidate matrix onto the PSD/secant-consistent set; rather it is a soft penalty term (Rsec) added to the meta-training loss that shapes the vector generator's outputs. This is fine as a design choice, but calling it a 'projection' and claiming it ensures 'theoretical soundness' and 'preserves core Quasi-Newton properties' overstates the guarantee—satisfaction of the secant condition is only approximate and only encouraged during training, not enforced at test time.

The efficiency narrative is internally inconsistent: Table 1 shows L-SR1 needs 13 inner iterations to reach its best PA-MPJPE versus 4 for LGD, while Table 2 reports per-iteration runtime (91ms vs 166ms). Multiplying these out, L-SR1's total inference time (~1.18s) is actually about 1.8x longer than LGD's (~0.66s) to reach its reported best result, which directly contradicts the paper's repeated claims of 'faster convergence' and is never discussed or reconciled in the text.

HMR evaluation includes only one learned-optimization baseline (LGD); stronger or more recent second-order-inspired learned optimizers cited in related work (e.g., Gärtner et al.'s transformer-based optimizer, Ayad et al.'s unrolled BFGS) are discussed qualitatively but not compared quantitatively, weakening the claim of outperforming 'existing learned optimization-based approaches.'

Analytic experiments are conducted at fairly small scale (training at N=2 for quadratics, N=100 for performance profiles) with modest test sets (30–32 problems), and no variance across multiple random seeds/training runs is reported for the main comparison plots (Fig. 3), making it hard to assess statistical robustness of the reported gains.
Notational inconsistency between the main paper (pk = xk − xk−1) and the appendix (pk = xk+1 − xk) for the secant-pair definitions could confuse readers trying to reproduce the method exactly.
Code is not yet released ('will be made publicly available'), so full reproducibility currently rests solely on the appendix descriptions.

The theoretical content (Lemma 1, positive-definiteness needed for descent direction) is standard textbook material restated rather than a new theoretical contribution, so the paper's claimed 'theoretical soundness' rests more on architectural design than new analysis.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored niche (learned second-order/quasi-Newton optimization) with a principled model-based deep learning design that embeds trainable rank-one updates inside the classical SR1 structure while preserving PSD-by-construction preconditioners.

The PGSM mechanism is a sensible, lightweight way to encourage secant consistency during meta-training without incurring an explicit projection subproblem at inference, and the paper provides a clear theoretical motivation (Eq. 6-9) connecting it to a least-squares PSD projection.

Extensive ablations are provided: buffer size sensitivity, cross-dimension generalization (N=2 to N=10), scalar vs. element-wise learning rates, encoder input/hidden-dimension ablations, and data-efficiency studies (training on fractions of AMASS) — these give useful insight into design choices and robustness.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility details: architecture tables, hyperparameter settings, and training protocols for each experiment are included in the appendix, along with runtime/memory profiling (Appendix A).

Real-world downstream evaluation on HMR (3DPW) shows the method outperforms the learned first-order baseline (LGD) and classical LBFGS/SPIN baselines with a smaller, more efficient model and no task-specific fine-tuning, which is a practically meaningful demonstration beyond toy benchmarks.
The limitations section is honest and specific about per-step cost, task-specific meta-training scope, and added hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly acknowledges that the composite update (PSD preconditioner combined with a per-coordinate learned learning-rate vector) is not guaranteed to be symmetric or to produce a descent direction, undermining the core theoretical selling point (PSD-by-construction) of the method; this gap is deferred entirely to empirical validation rather than resolved analytically.

The closest and most directly comparable prior work, the Transformer-based learned second-order optimizer of Gärtner et al. (2023), which is discussed extensively and contrasted conceptually throughout the paper (e.g., regarding naive vv^T PSD updates), is never empirically compared against in any experiment (quadratics, performance profiles, or HMR), leaving the central comparative claim (that PGSM improves over prior PSD-based learned second-order approaches) empirically unsupported.

On the very problem class SR1/QN methods are designed for (quadratics), classical LBFGS still outperforms L-SR1 with PGSM (Fig. 3a), which somewhat undercuts the practical value proposition of the learned approach for exactly the setting where second-order methods should excel; the advantage is confined to non-convex/diverse benchmark suites and the downstream HMR task.

Analytic experiments are trained and evaluated in fairly low dimensions (N=2 training, N=10 test for the core quadratic study), and cross-task generalization is not tested with a single unified model — each task family (quadratic, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin) requires separate meta-training, which limits the generality claims made in the introduction and conclusion.

Some reported comparisons rely on small differences that may not be statistically meaningful (e.g., Table 3 reports a 0.22mm PA-MPJPE difference between scalar and vector learning-rate variants) yet are used to support qualitative claims about coordinate-wise adaptation being beneficial for structured problems.

The project page/code link placeholder in the implementation section appears empty, raising concern about code availability and full reproducibility despite otherwise detailed hyperparameter reporting.

HMR results, while better than the learned-optimization baselines used, remain far behind modern regression-based SOTA (e.g., WHAM, PromptHMR), and while the paper reasonably frames this as a different efficiency/data regime, the practical significance of the accuracy gap relative to these methods is not fully contextualized.
